summary: A proposal to start discussion on a network Data Management System, or Data Control Facility, building on tools like NCP and Telnet. It is a framework, not a full design, aimed at letting users share data more easily.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 304 sketches a service for finding and moving data between network computers. It sets out parts that could work together, while leaving many design questions open for discussion.

questions: what is the data control facility
how would the network catalog locate data
subtitle: A framework for sharing and managing data across the network

tldr.problem: The proposal seeks a coordinated way for users to find, describe, convert and transfer data held at different network sites.
tldr.mechanism: It sketches a Data Control Facility that coordinates a catalog, data conversion services, remote facilities and file transfer, building on existing network tools.
tldr.outcome: The author presents a framework for discussion, not a complete protocol or final design.

today: RFC 304 is a proposal for network data management. Its text explicitly presents a framework for discussion rather than an exhaustive design.

sections.title: A Proposal, Not a Finished Protocol
sections.content:
The author presents this document as a starting framework for discussing a network Data Management System, also called a Data Control Facility (DCF). Its goal is to coordinate tools that let users share data. The proposal builds on existing services such as NCP, Telnet and the Form Machine.

It does not define a complete protocol or promise access to every database. It focuses on data that has been described and listed in the network catalog.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is an early plan, not a finished set of rules. It proposes combining existing network tools to help users work with listed data.

sections.title: The Main Parts of the Service
sections.content:
The design identifies a Telnet user interface, a coordinating DCF, a network catalog, a Form Machine for data conversion, remote DCF processes and a file transfer protocol. Together these parts would accept a user's request, locate the data, convert it when needed and arrange its transfer between sites.

The catalog would record data descriptions and physical locations. The proposal considers local and distributed directory information, with copies at sites that hold network data.
sections.plainLanguage: A user would make a request through a command interface. A coordinator would find the data, arrange any needed format change, and ask the file-transfer service to move it.

sections.title: Describing and Selecting Data
sections.content:
The proposal draws on the Data Language, which describes data as named containers that can be nested inside other containers. Examples of container types in the text include STRING, INT, REAL, ARRAY, LIST and STRUCT. Names can reflect the nesting of the data.

Operations such as assignment, selection by element number, adding and deleting are discussed. Selecting a subset would let a user request only the relevant part of a larger file.
sections.plainLanguage: Data can be named and organized in nested groups. A user could identify a particular part of a larger collection instead of transferring all of it.

sections.title: Conversion and File Transfer
sections.content:
The Form Machine could convert data to a format required by a receiving program. The proposed DCF would call stored forms when possible, while specialized transformations could still be written and run by users. File transfer between DCFs would carry the data and return acknowledgments to the coordinating DCF.

The proposal closes by asking the network community to develop the ideas into a coordinated specification and implementation effort.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers use different data formats, a conversion service could reshape the data before transfer. The author asks others to help develop this plan further.
